h1: Olive Oil for Bread: Dipping, Za'atar and How Much to Pour
excerpt: A saucer of unheated oil and a torn piece of bread is the plainest test an olive oil ever gets, and the easiest one to set badly.
keyTakeaway: Olive oil for bread is the use where least hides the oil: no heat, no acid, no garlic. Serve it at room temperature in a shallow saucer, pour a tablespoon at a time and refill, tear an open-crumbed bread rather than cutting it, and keep za'atar and dukkah in separate bowls.
heroAlt: Olive oil pouring in a steady stream from a stainless steel pipe into an open vat, the surface below already covered in green-gold oil.
inlineAlt: A small white saucer of green olive oil on a wooden board, with torn pieces of flatbread beside it and a spoon holding dried thyme.
intro: Bread and a saucer of olive oil is one of the oldest ways to serve it and the hardest to hide behind. Nothing is heated, nothing is cut with vinegar, nothing is buried under garlic.
Which bread holds oil, what za'atar, dukkah and balsamic each do to a saucer, what temperature to serve at, and how much to pour.

sections.heading: Why an unheated saucer shows the oil's character

blocks.text: Dipping is the use where least happens to the oil. Heat drives off the volatile compounds carrying the grassy and peppery notes, and a dressing cuts them with acid and salt. On bread the oil arrives whole: fruit first, then bitterness, then pepper at the back of the throat.
A saucer is unforgiving of a tired bottle: oil that stood open beside the stove since March reads flat here.

sections.heading: The bread matters as much as the oil

blocks.text: Bread decides how much oil reaches you and in what state. An open, chewy crumb takes a measured amount and holds its shape to your mouth. A soft sandwich loaf wets straight through and turns greasy; a dry cracker snaps and leaves the oil behind.

items: **Arabic flatbread, pita or saj.** Tear it; a torn edge holds more oil.
**Sourdough or a country loaf.** Open crumb takes oil, crust gives you a grip.
**Warm roti canai or naan.** Fine, but they carry their own fat, so pour less.
**Soft sandwich bread.** Skip it: soaks through and tears.

sections.heading: Za'atar, dukkah and balsamic pull three ways

blocks.text: Three additions take a saucer three different places. Za'atar turns it herbal and sour, with thyme, sumac and sesame. Dukkah turns it nutty and crunchy, a dry mix of toasted nuts and seeds. Balsamic turns it sharp and never mixes: the vinegar sits under the oil in beads.

items: **Za'atar.** A teaspoon per tablespoon of oil, left five minutes.
**Dukkah.** Keep it dry in its own bowl; press oiled bread into it.
**Balsamic.** Oil first, vinegar dropped in the centre, no stirring.
**Flaky salt and cracked pepper.** Changes the oil least.
**Chilli flakes with lemon zest.** Bright and hot, good with a green oil.

blocks.text: The same pairing is sold ready made as [wild thyme infused olive oil](/products/infused-extra-virgin-olive-oil-wild-thyme), the leaf steeped into the oil rather than spooned on top.

sections.heading: Serving temperature and how much to pour

blocks.text: Serve olive oil for bread at room temperature, which a Malaysian kitchen manages without help. A bottle straight from the refrigerator is the problem: cold oil goes cloudy, thickens and gives up almost no aroma. Take it out an hour ahead and pour a shallow layer.

sections.heading: Setting a dipping course for guests

blocks.text: A dipping course takes two minutes and one decision: the oil goes out plain first and everything else follows. Guests who have tasted the oil alone know what they are dipping into, and the za'atar bowl stops being the only thing they remember.

items: Warm the bread two minutes in a dry pan, then wrap it.
Pour a shallow layer into a white saucer so the colour shows.
Set za'atar, dukkah and salt in separate bowls, not in the oil.
Tear the bread at the table; cut bread dries waiting.
Refill from the bottle; never leave a deep saucer standing.

blocks.text: Most dipping saucers fail for reasons unrelated to the recipe. A saucer poured an hour before anyone sits down has been meeting air the whole time. A bottle kept above the stove was finished before it reached the table. Bread from a plastic bag pulls apart.
The oil you would taste plain is the one worth a saucer. See [what cold-pressed olive oil really means](/blog/what-cold-pressed-olive-oil-really-means) and the [bottles and sizes](/products).
Room temperature, a shallow white saucer, a tablespoon at a time, bread torn rather than sliced. Taste the oil plain first, keep za'atar and dukkah in their own bowls, and refill.

faqs.q: What olive oil is best for dipping bread?
faqs.a: Extra virgin, because dipping leaves the oil less masked than any other use. Refined and pure grades have had the aromatic compounds stripped out and give a saucer little to taste. Freshness counts as much as grade: a recently opened bottle reads brighter than an old one.

faqs.q: How much olive oil goes in a dipping saucer?
faqs.a: About a tablespoon per person, as a shallow layer rather than a deep pool. A thin layer in a wide saucer meets a lot of air, so pour small amounts and refill from the bottle instead of filling the saucer once at the start.

faqs.q: Should olive oil for bread be warmed?
faqs.a: No. Room temperature is where the aroma is fullest, and heating a saucer drives off the volatile compounds you are serving it for. If the bottle has been in a refrigerator, leave it on the counter an hour rather than putting it near a flame.

faqs.q: How do you make a za'atar and olive oil dip?
faqs.a: Pour a shallow layer of oil into a saucer, add roughly a teaspoon of za'atar per tablespoon of oil, stir once and leave five minutes so the sumac and thyme loosen. Serve with torn flatbread, pressed into the saucer rather than dragged through it.

faqs.q: Why does balsamic vinegar sit under the olive oil?
faqs.a: Vinegar is water-based and denser than oil, so it sinks and stays as separate dark beads unless something is whisked in to hold the two together. On a dipping saucer that separation is the point: each piece of bread takes a different ratio.

faqs.q: Which bread is best with olive oil?
faqs.a: An open, chewy crumb with a real crust: Arabic flatbread, sourdough, a country loaf, or a baguette cut on the diagonal. Soft sandwich bread wets through and falls apart in the saucer, and dry crackers snap before taking up much oil at all.
